headline: High-risk filesystem and MCP interaction: Continue can write/read workspace files and use MCP, while marker is local-only and non-networked, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways through shared files.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, so attacker-controlled document content from marker can be fed back into Continue through shared files or exported artifacts. marker itself has no tool use, but its document-processing output can still carry malicious instructions. This is a plausible default pathway, though not as direct as a shared MCP bridge.
conditions: IF marker processes attacker-controlled documents that are later opened in Continue's workspace
IF Continue ingests file content as trusted instructions or MCP payloads
mitigations: Disable automatic opening of marker outputs in Continue
Keep marker outputs in a separate directory from active coding work
Review any document text before pasting or importing into Continue
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for files passed between tools

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and can write/read workspace files; marker is a document processor with no declared filesystem or network surfaces, so the main leakage path is shared workspace content rather than direct exfiltration. The blast radius can include sensitive code or documents if both operate on the same folder.
conditions: IF marker is run on the same workspace containing sensitive source code or editor buffers
IF Continue writes generated content back into that shared workspace
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for code and documents
Restrict marker to non-sensitive inputs
Turn off automatic sync of generated files into the coding workspace
Delete temporary outputs after processing

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue has filesystem write and broad network egress, while marker has no write, network, or subprocess capabilities. There is no strong write-write conflict, but both can touch the same files if co-located, so the overlap is limited and mostly one-sided.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF Continue modifies files that marker is simultaneously reading or transforming
mitigations: Avoid concurrent runs on the same directory
Serialize edits through one operator-controlled step
Use read-only inputs for marker
requires-engineering: add file locks or workspace partitioning

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or instructions that marker may later transform into documents, and marker's outputs may be treated as authoritative artifacts by the operator. Because marker has no verification or action-taking safeguards in the profile, errors can cascade from Continue into downstream document outputs, though not into direct external actions.
conditions: IF Continue-generated text is used as source material for marker
IF the operator treats marker output as a final authoritative document without review
mitigations: Require human review of Continue output before document generation
Compare marker output against source text for critical sections
Keep a changelog of transformed content
requires-engineering: add verification checksums between stages

E_compliance.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers and may send data to a user-chosen model provider, while marker is a local document-processing tool with no declared network egress. The main compliance concern is a residency or retention mismatch if sensitive code is routed through Continue's external provider; marker is not the primary compliance driver here.
conditions: IF Continue is configured to send sensitive code or buffers to a third-party model provider
IF the processed documents contain regulated data
mitigations: Use a local model provider for Continue
Avoid sending regulated data through Continue
Review provider retention settings before use
requires-engineering: document a data-flow policy for both tools
